title: What's new in DAW Pro: tune a voice, sing your words
_doc: Stages in order. TALK = narration (vo/<id>.wav) over `shots`, cut on sentences by `cutOn` (sentence indices, resolved to `cutAt` seconds by sync-cuts.mjs from the take's own pauses). PLAY = loops/<loop> under bursts/<burst>/clip.mp4 (a screen take trimmed to the excerpt's first sample: sync-takes.py). Every play beat sets normalize:false — its level was set ONCE by cut-loops.py (an A/B pair shares one gain). Shots resolve against out/shots. Every number spoken is in work/measure/summary.json or loops/cuts.json, measured off the renders of the saved states that play under it.

stages.narration: This is DAW Pro. We'll write a short song, give it words, have the app sing them, and then tune that voice. Nobody sang into a microphone: the singer is DAW Pro's built-in voice, running on this Mac. Here's where we're headed.

We start from an empty project. Drums first, from DAW Pro's own drum machine with its 909 kit. The step grid shows eight named rows, Kick up to Cymbal, and a new Accent row underneath: click a step there and every hit in it plays harder. I've left it empty.
Then a bass, and a soft pad playing four chords: B minor, G, D and A, round and round. That's the whole band.
The tune gets its own track, called Lead: thirty-two notes across eight bars. For now, an electric piano plays it.

Now the words. Right-click the melody and choose Sing these notes. The sheet has three parts: Words, Voice and Height. I typed four lines of my own, one syllable per note. Height says the tune fits the voice. I add a harmony, a third above, and the sheet works out the key by itself: D major.

Press Sing it, and a card shows which line is being sung and roughly how long is left. It says Agent because I started this take from a script; the job is the same. Both parts took thirty-seven seconds.
Two new tracks arrive: the lead vocal, and the harmony a third above. From here on the piano is muted, so the voice is on top.

Open the vocal in the note editor. It found thirty-three notes, plus twenty-one sounds with no pitch, like breaths, drawn as striped boxes. The white line is the pitch the singer actually sang. With Hear on, pressing a note plays just that note.
The Split tool shows its cut line before you cut. Here it would make two halves, of four hundred and ninety-six milliseconds each.

Now I'll spoil this take on purpose, so there's something to fix. I select the last note of each line and drag one up, and the other three follow. Holding Option lets them sit between the keys: seventy cents sharp, about three quarters of a semitone. Measured on the sound, they now sit between sixty-five and seventy-six cents sharp. Listen to the line endings.

Tune to Melody puts them back. Right-click the vocal, then Tune Vocal, then Tune to Melody. Each sung note moves to the melody note under it, and it found the right melody, Lead. Because I moved notes by hand, it asks first: replace your hand edits? Yes. Tuned twenty-nine notes to Lead.
Here are the first two lines, before and after. Their two spoiled notes go from seventy-five and sixty-five cents sharp, to seven and zero.

Tuning has styles. Natural, the one we used: every note lands in tune, and it still sounds like singing. Hard Tune: holds each note in tune, with less vibrato, the robot effect. Vibrato is the small wobble on a long note. The editor draws Hard Tune's notes almost flat, but measured on the sound it removes about half the wobble: on nine long notes, from seventy-eight cents top to bottom, down to thirty-eight. It's subtle on this voice, so here it is alone: Natural, then Hard Tune.

Next, a big move: every note dragged down an octave. Keep voice size, at a hundred percent, keeps the voice its own size when notes move. Turned off, the voice follows the note. The editor warns it can sound squeaky, but that's for a jump up; going down, it turns into a slowed-down giant. Measured with it off, the centre of the voice's sound drops to fifty-three percent, like a tape at half speed, which measures fifty-four. At a hundred percent it stays at ninety-five. First off, then on.

The Voice tool does this on purpose, one note at a time: drag a note down for a deeper voice, up for a brighter one, and the note itself stays. I made the whole last line deeper, by six. Measured, the centre of its sound drops fourteen percent, and the pitch doesn't move. It also gets quieter: the voice alone by about four decibels, the whole song by just over one. The last line, before and after.
That's what's new for voices: your words sung on your melody, a note editor you can hear, Tune to Melody, Hard Tune, and a voice that keeps its size. Here's the finished song.
